clue.text: Rumoured to betray Irish playwright

indicators.note: rumoured means passed on by word of mouth, so we want a word that sounds like one meaning 'to betray'

parts.note: to sing is slang for informing on accomplices, so betraying them

explanation.surface: Gossip says someone is about to inform on an Irish dramatist.
explanation.walkthrough: J. M. Synge wrote The Playboy of the Western World; his name is said just like SING, the slang for turning informer.
explanation.definitionFit: John Millington Synge was a leading dramatist of the Irish literary revival.

clue.text: Multiple prize-winning tragedian confuses chess with polo

indicators.note: confuses means mixes up, so the letters of the two games are jumbled together

explanation.surface: An award-winning tragic writer mixes up two games.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confuses' scrambles CHESS and POLO together; Sophocles won the Athenian drama prize many times.
explanation.definitionFit: Sophocles, the Athenian tragic poet, won first prize at the Dionysia many times.

clue.text: Alan Paton's birthplace was like everyone else's

explanation.surface: The South African novelist was born in an ordinary way.
explanation.walkthrough: Alan Paton was born in Pietermaritzburg in the province of Natal; 'was' joins the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Paton came from the South African province of that name, and as an adjective it means relating to one's birth, which everyone shares.

clue.text: Gertrude Stein seems to have written his autobiography

definitions.text: Gertrude Stein seems to have written his autobiography

parts.words: Gertrude Stein seems to have written his autobiography
parts.note: Stein followed The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas with a book called the autobiography of all people in general, so the clue treats that as a person

explanation.surface: A suggestion that Gertrude Stein ghost-wrote some man's life story.
explanation.walkthrough: Stein's 1937 book is Everybody's Autobiography; the clue pretends its subject is one man.
explanation.definitionFit: Stein's 1937 memoir title names all people collectively as its supposed subject.

clue.text: "Poetry is what happens when an anxiety meets a " (Lawrence Durrell)

definitions.text: "Poetry is what happens when an anxiety meets a " (Lawrence Durrell)

parts.words: "Poetry is what happens when an anxiety meets a " (Lawrence Durrell)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank clue: the missing last word of Durrell's remark about poetry, the craft or skill an anxious writer brings to bear

explanation.surface: A quotation from Lawrence Durrell with its final word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Durrell's saying ends with the word for a practised method or skill; the solver simply completes the quotation.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word in Durrell's remark names the practised skill or method of a craft.

clue.text: Mark's nephew recalls Scott's hermit

explanation.surface: King Mark's nephew brings to mind a hermit in a Scott novel.
explanation.walkthrough: In the legend, Tristan is nephew of King Mark of Cornwall; Scott's Quentin Durward features Tristan l'Hermite, so the 'hermit' is his surname. 'recalls' joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: The lover of Isolde is King Mark's nephew, and Scott's provost marshal Tristan l'Hermite bears the name.

clue.text: Arrived with sale item at court

parts.note: arrived means came
a lot is an item put up at auction

explanation.surface: Someone turned up with something for auction at a royal court.
explanation.definitionFit: Camelot is the legendary seat of King Arthur and his court.

clue.text: Dickensian clerk said to be a different chap

definitions.text: Dickensian clerk said to be a different chap

parts.words: Dickensian clerk said to be a different chap
parts.note: the clerk in Nicholas Nickleby has the first name Newman, which spoken is 'new man', a different chap

explanation.surface: A clerk in Dickens is reported to be someone else entirely.
explanation.walkthrough: Newman Noggs is Ralph Nickleby's clerk; his first name sounds like 'new man'.
explanation.definitionFit: Newman Noggs is Ralph Nickleby's downtrodden clerk in Nicholas Nickleby.

clue.text: Clue like 26 might be too quaint

indicators.note: might be suggests the letters could form something else when rearranged

explanation.surface: A clue of the kind at 26 could be overly old-fashioned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'might be' rearranges TOO QUAINT; 26 across is built on a quotation from A. J. P. Taylor.
explanation.definitionFit: 26 across is a fill-in built around cited words, so it is a clue of that kind.

clue.text: Bell, perhaps, living near Acton

parts.note: the Brontë sisters wrote as Currer, ... and Acton Bell, so a Bell beside Acton is another of the pen-names

explanation.surface: Someone called Bell who lives near Acton in west London.
explanation.walkthrough: Acton reads as the London district but is Anne Brontë's pen-name Acton Bell; Emily wrote as Ellis Bell.
explanation.definitionFit: Emily Brontë published as Ellis Bell, alongside her sister Anne's pseudonym Acton Bell.

clue.text: Rose Macaulay's contribution to gamesmanship?

parts.note: Rose Macaulay wrote a 1920 novel with this title, and Stephen Potter wrote the book Gamesmanship, so his doctrine would be named after him with an -ism ending

explanation.surface: A question about what the novelist Rose Macaulay added to the art of winning games by ploys.
explanation.walkthrough: Two readings meet: the title of Macaulay's satirical novel, and a joke coinage for the teachings of Stephen Potter, author of Gamesmanship.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the title of Macaulay's satire on popular journalism, and punningly the creed of Stephen Potter's Gamesmanship.

clue.text: Michael Slade's fiend arising from disturbed lough ()

indicators.note: disturbed means stirred up, so the letters of the following word are rearranged

explanation.surface: A horror novelist's monster rises from a churned-up Irish lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disturbed' rearranges LOUGH, an Irish lake; Michael Slade's thriller is titled Ghoul.
explanation.definitionFit: Michael Slade's horror novel takes its title from a grave-robbing demon of folklore.

clue.text: Alternative sort of landscape line on Trollope farm

parts.note: or introduces an alternative
a ley line is a supposed alignment of ancient sites across the landscape

explanation.surface: A line across the land runs over a farm in a Trollope novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Trollope's novel Orley Farm supplies the definition; 'on' just sets the line after the alternative.
explanation.definitionFit: Orley Farm is the property at the heart of Anthony Trollope's 1862 novel of that title.

clue.text: The charms of Scott and Burrow

definitions.text: The charms of Scott and Burrow

parts.words: The charms of Scott and Burrow
parts.note: lucky amulets, and also the title Scott gave to one of his crusading novels, plural because a second author is added

explanation.surface: An appreciation of the appeal of two writers named Scott and Burrow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charms' looks like personal appeal but means amulets; Scott's novel The Talisman is the literary hook.
explanation.definitionFit: Amulets thought to bring luck are charms, and Scott wrote a crusader novel with the singular as title.

clue.text: Simpleton holds current measure for pointed mockery

indicators.note: holds means one word grips another inside it

parts.note: a loon is a foolish person
the amp is the unit measuring electric current

explanation.surface: A fool grips an ammeter while being sharply ridiculed.
explanation.definitionFit: A satirical piece ridiculing someone is a form of sharp mockery.

clue.text: A month at sea for Brideshead character

parts.note: March is a month of the year
the main is a poetic word for the open sea

explanation.surface: A month spent at sea for a figure in Waugh's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at' just links the month and the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Marchmain is Sebastian's father in Evelyn Waugh's Brideshead Revisited.

clue.text: It characterizes Logan Pearsall Smith's work

definitions.text: It characterizes Logan Pearsall Smith's work

parts.words: It characterizes Logan Pearsall Smith's work
parts.note: Logan Pearsall Smith published a book of short aphoristic pieces titled Trivia, so the adjective from that title describes it

explanation.surface: A description of the writing of the essayist Logan Pearsall Smith.
explanation.walkthrough: Smith's best-known book is Trivia, so its adjective sums up his work, with a sly dig at its slightness.
explanation.definitionFit: Smith's collection was called Trivia, and the related adjective means slight or unimportant.

clue.text: Exceptionally durable academicians?

parts.note: members of the Académie française are nicknamed 'les immortels', and the clue reads that as long-lasting scholars

explanation.surface: A question about remarkably long-lived scholars.
explanation.walkthrough: The forty members of the Académie française are traditionally called the immortals.
explanation.definitionFit: The forty members of the Académie française are nicknamed for their supposed undying fame.

clue.text: He did not hold Arcadia, nor Walden, anyhow

indicators.note: anyhow means in any haphazard way, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Neither Arcadia nor Walden belonged to him in any case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anyhow' scrambles NOR WALDEN; the definition is playful: imaginary Arcadia and Thoreau's Walden were no one's property.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who holds property in land is defined by contrast with ideal places no proprietor ever owned.

clue.text: A yarn so tangled from dramatist

indicators.note: a tangled yarn is a knotted mess, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A knotted story comes from a playwright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tangled' scrambles A YARN SO; William Saroyan was an American playwright.
explanation.definitionFit: William Saroyan was an American playwright, author of The Time of Your Life.

clue.text: Shakespearean clerk seen as siren going up in the world

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means the letters are read from bottom to top

explanation.surface: A clerk in Shakespeare is seen as a temptress who rises socially.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going up in the world' reverses AS SIREN in this down clue; Nerissa disguises herself as a lawyer's clerk in The Merchant of Venice.
explanation.definitionFit: In The Merchant of Venice, Portia's maid Nerissa disguises herself as a lawyer's clerk.

clue.text: Crime writer concealed in some inn

indicators.note: the writer's name lies concealed in the letters of the following words, though scrambled rather than in a run

explanation.surface: A detective novelist hides out in a country pub.
explanation.walkthrough: Despite 'concealed in', SOME INN holds the letters in a jumble, not a straight run, so they must be rearranged; Georges Simenon created Maigret.
explanation.definitionFit: Georges Simenon was the Belgian novelist who created Inspector Maigret.

clue.text: Framework lacking direction for satirical poet

indicators.note: lacking means without, so a letter is taken out

parts.note: a skeleton is a supporting framework
E is east, a compass direction

explanation.surface: A structure missing a guiding sense belongs to a mocking poet.
explanation.walkthrough: John Skelton was a Tudor poet known for his biting satire.
explanation.definitionFit: John Skelton was the Tudor court poet known for biting satirical verse.

clue.text: 15 works of Nabokov? Or some of his collected specimens?

explanation.surface: Were Nabokov's slight writings, or the insects he collected, short-lived things?
explanation.walkthrough: 15 is TRIVIAL: trivial works are short-lived writings; Nabokov was a keen butterfly collector, and the plural also names mayflies.
explanation.definitionFit: Short-lived trifling writings are one sense, and in zoology the word names mayflies, the kind of insect a lepidopterist might pin.

clue.text: Farrier's death thus affected Hopkins's duty ()

definitions.text: Farrier's death thus affected Hopkins's duty

parts.words: Farrier's death thus affected Hopkins's duty
parts.note: in Hopkins's poem Felix Randal, the priest learns the farrier is dead and says his duty is all finished

explanation.surface: The death of a blacksmith altered the poet Hopkins's obligations.
explanation.walkthrough: Felix Randal opens with the line 'Felix Randal the farrier, O is he dead then? my duty all ended'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hopkins's poem says his pastoral duty was all over once the farrier died.

clue.text: Australian army allocation includes one familiar with Chatwin's Songlines ()

indicators.note: includes means the run of letters sits within the words that follow

explanation.surface: Australian military rations cover a man who knows Chatwin's book on Aboriginal song paths.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Australian' flags the word as Australian English: a myall is an Aboriginal person living traditionally, someone who knows the songlines of Chatwin's book.
explanation.definitionFit: A myall is an Aboriginal person living in the traditional way, who would know the ancestral song paths.

clue.text: Short-fused Verona teenager gets nothing on capital ( )

indicators.note: in an across clue, one piece on another means it comes after it

parts.note: Rome is the capital city of Italy
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A hot-headed young man from Verona sets his sights on the capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's impetuous young lover from Verona is famously quick to act and quick to fight.

clue.text: State of Eberhart's verse

parts.note: the American poet Richard Eberhart summered on this New England coast and set many poems there, so it is his poetic state

explanation.surface: A comment on the condition of Eberhart's poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' looks like condition but means a US state; Eberhart wrote often of the Maine coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Eberhart's poems often celebrate the New England state where he spent summers.

clue.text: Tot a theatre may present ()

parts.note: a tot is a small measure of spirits, a dram

explanation.surface: A child that a theatre could put on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tot' reads as a small child but is a small drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A play is the kind of serious work a theatre stages.

clue.text: A.J. P. Taylor said that Mussolini was a great showman whose 4 Ac improved as the real — deteriorated

definitions.text: A.J. P. Taylor said that Mussolini was a great showman whose 4 Ac improved as the real — deteriorated

parts.words: A.J. P. Taylor said that Mussolini was a great showman whose 4 Ac improved as the real — deteriorated
parts.note: a fill-in: Taylor's remark contrasts Mussolini's stagecraft (4 across) with the real state of affairs, the word for circumstances filling the dash

explanation.surface: A historian's quip that Mussolini's showmanship grew as his true position worsened.
explanation.walkthrough: 4 Ac is TECHNIQUE; the dash wants the word for the actual state of affairs.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means the state of affairs or circumstances one is in.

clue.text: Son of king of Scotland, and Albion perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps suggests a possible rearrangement of the letters before it

explanation.surface: A Scottish prince is linked with the old name for Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges AND ALBION; Donalbain is Duncan's younger son in Macbeth.
explanation.definitionFit: In Macbeth, Donalbain is the younger son of King Duncan of Scotland.

clue.text: Direct artist ()

explanation.surface: An instruction to guide a painter.
explanation.walkthrough: Philip Wilson Steer was an English Impressionist painter.
explanation.definitionFit: To guide or direct a course, and the surname of the English painter Philip Wilson Steer.
